strong.text: You read this obstruction module the way a good registrar reads a case: setting, level, strangulation, then the plan. No core objective came out as a gap. Keep the review cards on their schedule, because the exam traps here (old keys, look-alike signs, timings) fade fast without repetition.

mixed.text: A solid base with some holes. Some objectives held up and some did not, and the pattern below shows which. Most misses in this topic come from one wrong model, such as a fixed rule applied to every setting, not from missing facts. Fix the models named below first, then use the cards.

weak.text: Several core objectives need rebuilding, and that is useful information, not a verdict. Obstruction rewards a few anchors: the level of the block, strangulation signs, and the rule that resuscitation comes first. Start with the review cards flagged below, in the order shown, and redo the module after a day.

secure.text: Most-common-cause questions held: you read the age, site and setting before answering, and you can give the old exam key and the current answer together.

shaky.text: Most-common-cause answers are partly there. Rebuild the grid: adult small bowel adhesions, then hernia; virgin abdomen hernia; adult large bowel carcinoma; 6 months to 2 years intussusception. Then add the PYQ key for India: hernia.

gap.text: You are giving one most-common-cause for every setting. Redo the PYQ-versus-current-practice card, then say it aloud: PYQs expected hernia in India, adhesions lead wherever abdominal surgery is common, carcinoma leads in large bowel.

secure.text: You sorted causes by their relation to the bowel wall, which lets you place a cause you have never memorised.

shaky.text: Sorting causes by wall relation is only partly secure. For each cause ask: inside the lumen, in the wall, or outside it? Gallstone and impaction are inside; carcinoma, strictures and intussusception are in the wall.

gap.text: Causes are sitting in your head as an unsorted list. Rebuild it with three boxes: intraluminal (impaction, gallstone, bezoar), intramural (tumour, stricture, atresia, intussusception), extramural (adhesions, hernia, volvulus, external compression).

secure.text: You derived the cardinal features from the level of the block rather than recalling a table, and you kept mechanical and adynamic obstruction apart.

shaky.text: The feature timeline is partly derived. Trace it each time: high small bowel block vomits early with little distension; large bowel block distends and becomes constipated early, vomiting late. Mechanical bowel sounds are tinkling; ileus is silent.

gap.text: The timeline of features is not yet logical for you. Ask how much bowel lies beyond the block. High block: vomiting early, distension minimal, constipation late. Large bowel block: constipation and distension early, vomiting late. Redo the features card.

secure.text: You picked out strangulation from the change in pain and the systemic signs, which is the skill that decides who goes to theatre.

shaky.text: Strangulation recognition is partly there. Anchor on the change: colic turning constant and severe, with tachycardia, fever, localised tenderness or guarding, leucocytosis and raised lactate.

gap.text: You are missing strangulation cues. Constant severe pain, tachycardia, fever, localised guarding and raised lactate mean ischaemic bowel, not simple obstruction. Reread the strangulation card and look for the changed pain word in every vignette.

secure.text: You told small from large bowel on film by the folds and the 3-6-9 numbers.

shaky.text: Plain-film reading is partly secure. Valvulae conniventes cross the full width in central small bowel; haustra do not in peripheral large bowel. The 3-6-9 numbers run small bowel, colon, caecum.

gap.text: Plain-film bowel identification needs rebuilding. Sketch both: central loops with folds that cross the lumen are small bowel; peripheral loops with partial folds are large bowel. Then attach 3, 6 and 9 cm to small bowel, colon and caecum.

secure.text: You separated the first test from the definitive one for obstruction and for paediatric intussusception.

shaky.text: Test ladders are partly secure. Plain film is first and shows that the bowel is obstructed; contrast CT is definitive in adult small bowel obstruction; ultrasound is the test for intussusception in a child.

gap.text: You are stopping at the first test or the therapeutic one. Write the ladder: plain film first, contrast CT for level, cause and strangulation, ultrasound for a child with intussusception. Barium by mouth is unsafe in perforation or large bowel obstruction.

secure.text: Imaging signs were matched to disease and modality correctly.

shaky.text: Sign matching is partly secure. Pair each sign with disease and test: coffee bean is sigmoid volvulus on plain film; bird's beak is volvulus on enema; claw is intussusception on enema; target is intussusception on ultrasound.

gap.text: The signs are mixed together in your memory. Make a four-column card: sign, disease, test, one-line cue. Coffee bean, bird's beak, claw, target and Rigler's triad each get one row.

secure.text: You handled the management order: resuscitate, screen for strangulation, hernia and closed loop, then allow a timed trial.

shaky.text: Management order is partly secure. Drip, suck and catheter first; theatre at once for strangulation, hernia or closed loop; otherwise adhesive obstruction gets a non-operative trial of about 72 hours, with contrast at 24 hours.

gap.text: The management sequence is out of order for you. Redo it as a flowchart: resuscitate, check for strangulation, hernia or closed loop, then trial, then the 24-hour contrast check and the 72-hour limit. The old dictum is quoted but current practice differs.

secure.text: You judged hernia risk by anatomy and kept the eponyms apart.

shaky.text: Hernia judgement is partly secure. Risk follows a narrow rigid neck, so femoral is highest among groin hernias. Richter traps part of the wall, Littre contains Meckel's diverticulum, Maydl has a W-shaped loop.

gap.text: Hernia risk and eponyms need a rebuild. Risk follows the neck, not frequency: femoral strangulates most. Then a three-line card: Richter equals partial wall, Littre equals Meckel's, Maydl equals W-shaped loop.

secure.text: You used age to choose between enema and resection in intussusception.

shaky.text: Intussusception management is partly secure. A stable child without peritonitis gets image-guided enema reduction; an adult usually has a lead point, often a tumour, so resection is chosen.

gap.text: Child and adult intussusception are blurred. Child: usually idiopathic and ileocolic, enema reduction unless peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction. Adult: pathological lead point, so resect. Redo that contrast card.

secure.text: You matched site to treatment for volvulus and obstructing cancer, and kept the caecum as the perforation site.

shaky.text: Site-specific treatment is partly secure. Sigmoid volvulus: scope detorsion, then elective colectomy. Caecal volvulus: right hemicolectomy. Right colon cancer: hemicolectomy; left: Hartmann's or selected anastomosis, with a stent as a bridge.

gap.text: Site and bowel state are not yet driving your treatment choice. Sigmoid and viable: detorse and later colectomy. Gangrene or caecum: resect. Right colon cancer: right hemicolectomy. Left: Hartmann's. The caecum perforates first because it is widest.

secure.text: Drug and treatment of choice for gallstone ileus, Ogilvie's and paralytic ileus were secure.

shaky.text: These one-line answers are partly secure. Gallstone ileus: enterolithotomy. Ogilvie's: correct the cause and electrolytes, then neostigmine with cardiac monitoring. Paralytic ileus: correct potassium, drip and suck.

gap.text: These answers need a quick card. Gallstone ileus: enterolithotomy, stone usually impacted in terminal ileum. Ogilvie's: neostigmine, with atropine ready. Paralytic ileus: hypokalaemia is the commonest metabolic cause, treated with drip and suck.

avoided.text: You kept the old exam key apart from current practice.

fell_recovered.text: You reached for adhesions first, then held both answers. That is the right fix, but the habit returns under time pressure. Read the setting words: for an India or developing-countries PYQ, hernia; for current practice, adhesions.

fell_open.text: You gave one most-common cause for every setting, so the old exam key and today's answer collided. Rehearse the pair: PYQs expected hernia in India; current practice says adhesions. Redo the PYQ-versus-current card.

avoided.text: You read the surgical history before naming a cause.

fell_recovered.text: You first named adhesions, then checked the history line. Keep that order under pressure: scars first. No previous surgery makes adhesions unlikely and points to hernia, then tumour.

fell_open.text: You defaulted to adhesions and skipped the line saying no previous surgery. Adhesions need an operated abdomen. In a virgin abdomen, examine every hernial orifice first. Revisit the operated-versus-virgin card.

avoided.text: You used age to choose the intussusception pathway.

fell_recovered.text: You applied the child's enema to an adult, then recovered. Under exam pressure, ask first: is there a lead point? An adult usually has one, often a tumour, so the answer is resection.

fell_open.text: You treated intussusception as one disease with one enema cure. Children are mostly idiopathic; adults usually have a pathological lead point, often a tumour. Redo the child-versus-adult contrast and say 'adult: look for tumour, resect'.

avoided.text: You checked peritonitis, perforation and shock before choosing theatre.

fell_recovered.text: You went to theatre first, then recognised that a stable child gets reduction. Under pressure the safe-feeling choice returns, so run the screen each time: peritonitis, perforation, shock, failed reduction.

fell_open.text: You treated surgery as the safest default for a child with intussusception. A resuscitated, stable child without peritonitis gets image-guided reduction first. Learn the four surgical triggers: peritonitis, perforation, shock, failed enema.

avoided.text: You separated the screening test from the definitive one.

fell_recovered.text: You stopped at a familiar test, then rebuilt the ladder. Remember: X-ray shows that it is obstructed, CT shows why. Under pressure the first test pulls hard.

fell_open.text: You treated the first or therapeutic test as the definitive one. Plain film shows the level; contrast CT is the investigation of choice in adult small bowel obstruction; ultrasound is chosen for a child with intussusception. Write the ladder from memory.

avoided.text: You matched each sign to its disease and modality.

fell_recovered.text: You blended two signs, then separated them. Hold the pairs: coffee bean is sigmoid volvulus on plain film; kidney-shaped caecum goes towards the left upper quadrant; claw on enema, target on ultrasound.

fell_open.text: You stored the imaging signs as one flat list. Each belongs to a disease and a test: coffee bean on plain film, bird's beak on enema, claw on enema, target and pseudokidney on ultrasound. Build a sign, disease, modality card.

avoided.text: You used the folds correctly to name the bowel.

fell_recovered.text: You swapped the markers, then fixed it. Keep the rule simple: valvulae cross the whole width in small bowel; haustra stop short in the large bowel.

fell_open.text: You treated valvulae conniventes and haustra as one group of folds. Valvulae conniventes cross the full width and mark small bowel; haustra do not and mark large bowel. Sketch the two bowels with their folds.

avoided.text: Your 3-6-9 numbers stayed attached to the right segments.

fell_recovered.text: You shuffled the numbers, then reanchored them. Under pressure, think calibre: 3 small bowel, 6 colon, 9 caecum, widening distally.

fell_open.text: You held 3, 6 and 9 as a rote string and shuffled the segments. Small bowel 3, colon 6, caecum 9, widening as you go distal. The widest segment perforates first. Redo the numbers card.

avoided.text: You kept frequency and risk apart.

fell_recovered.text: You equated the commonest hernia with the most dangerous, then corrected. Read the exact qualifier: 'most common' is not 'most likely to strangulate'.

fell_open.text: You read 'most' as one scale, so the commonest groin hernia became the riskiest. Strangulation risk follows a narrow rigid neck, so femoral leads. Pair each superlative with its exact qualifier.

avoided.text: You matched hernia eponyms to their contents.

fell_recovered.text: You first expected a classic complete obstruction picture, then adjusted. Richter strangulates part of the wall without obstructing; do not wait for vomiting.

fell_open.text: You assumed strangulation always means complete obstruction and blurred the eponyms. Richter traps part of the wall and can strangulate without obstructing; Littre contains Meckel's diverticulum; Maydl has a W-shaped loop. Make a three-row eponym card.

avoided.text: You derived the feature timeline from the level of the block.

fell_recovered.text: You filled the grid wrongly, then derived it. Keep deriving: ask how much bowel lies beyond the block.

fell_open.text: You memorised the feature grid without the logic and reversed it. Bowel below a small bowel block still empties, so constipation is late; a large bowel block leaves little distal bowel, so constipation is early. High block vomits early. Re-derive it on paper.

avoided.text: You separated working peristalsis from failed peristalsis.

fell_recovered.text: You thought silence meant a block, then reversed it. Mechanical obstruction is loud and tinkling; a silent abdomen suggests ileus or late peritonitis.

fell_open.text: You assumed a blocked gut is silent. In mechanical obstruction peristalsis fights a fixed block, so sounds are hyperactive and high-pitched; silence suggests paralytic ileus or late peritonitis. Reread the working-versus-failed gut contrast.

avoided.text: You read the site and the bowel state before choosing the volvulus operation.

fell_recovered.text: You applied one volvulus rule, then added site and bowel state. Under pressure: viable sigmoid, scope then colectomy; gangrene or caecum, resect.

fell_open.text: You used one rule, detorse, for every volvulus. Viable sigmoid: scope and flatus tube, then elective colectomy. Gangrene or perforation: Hartmann's. Caecal volvulus: right hemicolectomy. Order the steps: viability, site, then definitive operation.

avoided.text: You caught the change in pain character.

fell_recovered.text: You read persistent colic as simple, then recognised strangulation. Under pressure, look for the word constant plus tachycardia or guarding.

fell_open.text: You treated colicky pain as a fixed label for simple obstruction and missed the change. Constant severe pain with tachycardia, fever or localised guarding signals strangulation and needs theatre. Reread the strangulation card.

avoided.text: You screened for strangulation, hernia and closed loop before waiting.

fell_recovered.text: You offered a conservative trial where it was unsafe, then corrected. Screen first; the 72-hour trial belongs only to uncomplicated adhesive obstruction.

fell_open.text: You applied the 72-hour trial to every obstruction. It applies only to adhesive obstruction without strangulation, hernia or closed loop; those go to theatre. Redo the override list: strangulation, obstructed hernia, closed loop, failed trial.

avoided.text: Your timings stayed attached to their decisions.

fell_recovered.text: You mixed up the timings, then anchored them. Timeline: 24 hours contrast check, 24 to 48 hours second look, 72 hours trial limit.

fell_open.text: You treated 24, 24 to 48 and 72 hours as interchangeable. Contrast at 24 hours checks for resolution, a planned second look is at 24 to 48 hours, and 72 hours ends the non-operative trial. Draw one timeline.

avoided.text: You resuscitated before anything else.

fell_recovered.text: You reached for theatre first, then reordered. Drip, suck and catheter come before any decision about operating.

fell_open.text: You treated the operation as the first act and resuscitation as optional. Fluids with potassium, nasogastric decompression and a urinary catheter come first, as vomiting and third-space loss leave the patient dry. Say 'drip and suck first' before each management vignette.

avoided.text: Your most-common answers held up.

fell_recovered.text: You stretched 'common' to 'most common', then corrected. Cause: carcinoma. Volvulus site: sigmoid. Perforation site: caecum.

fell_open.text: You stretched a familiar large bowel condition to 'most common' and merged two caecal facts. Carcinoma is the commonest cause; sigmoid the commonest volvulus site; caecum the commonest perforation site. Keep the three separate.

avoided.text: You used the side of the tumour to choose the operation.

fell_recovered.text: You used one cancer operation, then used the site. Right: hemicolectomy with anastomosis. Left: Hartmann's, or selected anastomosis, with a stent as a bridge.

fell_open.text: You used one operation for every obstructing colon cancer. Name the side first: right gets hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis; left gets Hartmann's, or primary anastomosis in selected stable patients; a stent is a bridge or palliation for left-sided disease.

avoided.text: You sorted causes by wall relation.

fell_recovered.text: You sorted by name, then used wall relation. For any cause ask: inside the lumen, in the wall, or outside it?

fell_open.text: You sorted causes by name or organ rather than by wall relation. Gallstone is intraluminal; intussusception and strictures are intramural; adhesions, hernia and volvulus are extramural. Ask inside, in or outside for every cause.

E1.text: You tend to merge look-alikes: signs, folds and eponyms stored as one group. Fix it with side-by-side cards that name the single discriminating feature, such as folds crossing the lumen or not, or the test on which a sign is seen.

E2.text: You tend to sort a list by name instead of by its logic. For this topic rebuild sets from the logic, such as inside, in, or outside the wall, then test yourself with which-is-not questions.

E3.text: You tend to reverse a mechanism: which end empties, or whether a blocked gut is loud or silent. Trace what happens above and below the block before filling any table.

E4.text: You tend to stretch a superlative beyond its qualifier. Commonest cause, commonest site, most likely to strangulate and most likely to perforate are different questions. Write the exact qualifier beside each answer.

E5.text: You tend to answer with one key when the old exam key and current practice differ. For these topics say both: 'PYQs expected X; current practice is Y', and be ready to give the one the question wants.

E6.text: You tend to swap numbers. Attach each figure to a meaning, such as 3-6-9 to bowel calibre, or 24, 24 to 48 and 72 hours to the decision each governs, then retest them in application questions.

E7.text: You tend to skip the qualifier in the stem: surgical history, age, setting, side of the colon, or the pain change. Underline it before choosing, and ask what the answer would be on the other side of it.

E8.text: You tend to pick a screening or familiar test where a definitive one is asked. Keep a ladder of tests with the question each answers, from plain film to CT to ultrasound in the child.

E9.text: You tend to get the order wrong, often reaching for theatre or a rule before the screen. Say the sequence aloud: resuscitate, check for strangulation, hernia and closed loop, then decide on trial or operation.

E10.text: You tend to attach an eponym to the wrong condition. Pair each with its contrasting partner, for example Richter with partial wall, Littre with Meckel's, Maydl with the W-shaped loop.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on several answers that were wrong. Those are the most valuable errors in this module, because a corrected confident error sticks best. Before tapping Sure, name the qualifier that decides the answer. Review the cards for those traps first.

underconfident.text: Several of your correct answers were tapped as Guessing. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Before you tap, name the one fact that decides the answer; when you can, tap Sure and test that judgement.

calibrated.text: Your confidence tracked your accuracy: Sure answers were right, and any Guessing answers mark what to review first. That is a useful revision signal, so trust it and start with the items you flagged.

hints_heavy.text: You opened three or more hints. Using hints is a legitimate strategy, but the cold questions show what you can do unaided. Redo the module in a day and try each probe before opening a hint.

hints_none.text: You used no hints, even on the questions you missed. A hint after a first miss costs less than a second wrong answer and gives you a different angle on the stem. Use one the next time you are stuck, then compare what it changed.

hinted_only.text: Some objectives were right only after a hint and never unaided. That means the idea is recognisable but not yet retrievable. Review those cards before you retry the module without hints.

fast_lane.text: You answered a diagnostic correctly and confidently and skipped a worked explanation. That is the right use of the fast lane. The traps still appear later, so stay alert for them.

gap.text: Work through the cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky objectives. Review them at 1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days. Redo the module in a week; the traps you fell into are the ones the exam is most likely to set again.

clear.text: No gaps and nothing shaky. Review the cards at 1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days to hold this, and test yourself on the PYQ-versus-current-practice pairs, which are the likeliest to slip.
